quotes.text: I remember being impressed by his sheer physicality. The guy could dance. He could hit backflips on-beat. His legs seemed to be made of rubber. Even more impressive: He could do all this without lip-syncing or losing his breath. He was an athlete.
This was a small-town teenager who just wanted to be Michael Jackson. For the first few years of his career, this was how the world viewed Chris Brown.

As a singer, Chris Brown wasn't anywhere near the level of Usher, but that didn't really matter. With "Yeah!," Usher had established a blueprint for hard, urgent, rap-adjacent club-pop, and you didn't have to sing as well as Usher to make a song like that. "Run It!" is Chris Brown's version of "Yeah!," right down to the exclamation point in the title.
Chris Brown recorded his self-titled 2006 debut album quickly, and he got the chance to work with plenty of that era's hitmaking songwriters and producers.
With Storch and Garrett, Chris Brown made a song that pretty much sounds just like "Yeah!," except without the Lil Jon intensity and with a crappier guest verse.
Abandoning his traditional R&B sound for the ever-present, and ever trendy, rap-sung delivery that has infested every genre of music like silverfish in your grandma's basement

his dismissal of traditional album structure – ignoring the usual 45-minute, 15 track design for 40-track behemoths that run nearly THREE HOURS. Great for boosting numbers on streaming sites and spamming Billboard charts, sure, not so great for producing solid bodies of work.
That said, during R&B's darkest era to date, Chris Brown has been the genre's biggest (and most years, ONLY) mainstream star.
That's what makes Breezy such a weird release. It inches Brown toward freshening up his sound and presentation … but then he gets cold feet and it's business as usual.
The warm island grooves FINALLY give CB a fresh landscape to explore, happily dragging him from the usual trap drums and debauchery.
The album finally begins to gel a bit in the second half, thanks again to a willingness to experiment.
It's great to hear Chris actually singing again (reminder: He's actually pretty good at it) and it's encouraging to hear a song that manages to be sexy without being cartoonishly crude.
this is my cousin's best project in years, thanks to his decision to finally step out of his comfort zone and try new things.

For better or worse, Chris Brown has been the face of mainstream R&B for more than a decade. And truly, his talent is undeniable. He's arguably the best male performer we have (though the resurgence of Usher Raymond has that crown in question). And he spent so much of the 2010s sounding like a Young Money rapper (call him Tyga BackWoods) that it's easy to forget that he's one of the better vocalists of his era.
Despite all those accolades, along with scores of No. 1 records, he continues to lack the one thing that every true R&B legend has on their resume – that one great album to cement his legacy.

Cousin Chris has spent the past six years playing the Streaming Game – dropping forgettable albums with bloated tracklists that pad his streaming numbers in the short term, but cripple his legacy long term.

The first half sets an acoustic, almost intergalactic feel as Breezy embraces the 11:11 theme. "Ten Toes" ramps up the intensity with CB dipping a bit back into this hip-hop swag bag. It's not all empty posturing though; he speaks candidly about battling anxiety, showing the growth his fans have been begging for years now.
"Sensational," which gleefully embraces the Afrobeats vibe. Let's be real – Afrobeats may be hot in the streets, but the sound itself is getting as played out in 2023 as New Jack Swing was in 1993.
Breezy sounds bored out of his mind thanks to the droning vocals effects on "Nightmares."
"Messed Up" is another showcase of growth as Chris atones for his sins and begs his girl "don't give up on me."
"Midnight Freak," an energetic throwback to Chris' prime. It wouldn't sound out of place in the Exclusive era.

"Moonlight." Feeling like it was plucked from the Alexander O'Neal segment of a 1980s quiet storm playlist, Chris floats over the most captivating production on the album. His vocals are effortless and the direction is just what a maturing R&B veteran of his stature should be embracing.

Though the production is much stronger this time around, there's not enough variety to keep things interesting. "Make Up Your Mind" is the same rap&B-styled stuff we've heard ad nauseum since the F.A.M.E. days.
